title: Like the full moon
hookLine: Punna is told to fill herself with good things, like the moon on the fifteenth night (Therigatha, Punna)
carry: a little more light each evening

cards: A thin curve of light low in the evening sky. The next night, a little wider. Then wider again.
Nothing is bolted onto the moon. Night by night, more of its face catches the light, until one night the whole round face is lit.
A short poem in the Therigatha is built on that picture, and it's spoken to a nun named Punna. Yesterday's poem pictured freedom as something drying out. Today's pictures it as something filling up.

teach.h: A NAME THAT SOUNDS LIKE FULL.
teach.b: First, the name. Some readers hear a play on it: in Pali, Punna sounds like the word for full. On that hearing, a woman called full is told how to become full.
The poem tells her to fill herself with good things, the good qualities of the teaching, like a vessel being filled. Third, the moon.

teach.h: LIKE THE MOON ON THE FIFTEENTH.
teach.b: She is to fill herself like the moon on the fifteenth night, the night it comes full. The moon doesn't get there by force. Fourth, the darkness.
With wisdom made full, the poem says, she will tear through the great mass of darkness.

A full moon lights a whole field at night, so you can see the path in front of you. That's what the poem promises wisdom does. Put the two poems side by side: herbs drying in a pot, a moon filling night by night.
One is about what goes out of a person, the craving losing its sap. The other is about what comes in, good qualities, growing steadily.
The Therigatha holds both pictures without choosing between them, and some teachers call letting go and filling up two sides of one path.
The full-moon nights had a place in the early sangha too: they were observance days, uposatha, when the community gathered.

how: In Theravada communities the full-moon day is an observance day, uposatha, when lay Buddhists may visit the temple, take extra precepts and listen to teaching, and verses like Punna's are read as pictures of gradual growth on the path.

o: the night of the new moon, kept as holy
a nun told to fill up like the full moon
a nun who prayed to the moon each night

p: a name that sounds like full

s: Punna's poem compares her to the sun at noon
it compares her to the moon on the fifteenth night, filling up until it's full.
the Therigatha pictures freedom both as drying out and as filling up
herbs dried in a pot in the first poem; a moon filling night by night in Punna's.

games.q: you're Punna. a voice tells you how to grow free. which picture does it give you?
o: empty yourself, like a bowl turned over.
fill yourself with good things, like the moon on the fifteenth night.
burn bright, like a fire on a hill.
games.why: fill yourself with good things, like the full moon, and with wisdom made full, tear through the darkness.

practice: Choose one small good thing you could add before tonight: a kind message, a short walk outside, a meal made with care, a page of something worth reading. See where it fits, the hour and the place.
Not a whole full moon today; just one night's more light.

wordCard.voice: Punna. The nun told to fill herself with good things the way the moon fills, until wisdom breaks through the dark. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the nun's name, Puṇṇā; puṇṇa is the Pali word for full.

carryVoice: Your line: a little more light each evening. Fullness comes a night at a time. See you tomorrow.
